name: Duster coat

image.caption: Duster coat used by one of the Younger Brothers

lead: The duster is a long, lightweight, loose-fitting coat, originally worn to keep trail and road dust off clothes. In current style discussion it is a way to add a long vertical line and a film-character presence to an outfit.
Its look was carried by Western films, Hong Kong action films and television characters, which periodically revived interest in it.

paras: It is worn as an outer layer over regular outfits, in canvas, linen, waxed cotton or leather; riding versions are slit up the back.
No health risks; the long cut and lightweight material suit certain climates and body proportions differently.

angle.text: Worn as an outer layer, the duster creates a long vertical line and a dramatic silhouette.

lead: The duster coat is a long, light, loose coat that started as protective outerwear for horsemen and early motorists. As a style, it adds a long vertical line and a distinctive silhouette over everyday clothes.[1]

Early dusters were full-length, light canvas or linen coats worn by American horsemen; later versions used oilcloth and waxed cotton.[1] Sergio Leone reintroduced them to Westerns in the 1960s, and the style influenced fashion in France, where the coats were nicknamed maxis.[1]
infobox: Leone Westerns, A Better Tomorrow, The Wire

paras: A light, loose, long coat; riding versions are slit to hip level at the back and sometimes have straps to hold flaps in place.[1]

Dusters were worn over clothes in open cars on dirt roads in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.[1] Leone's team found the coats used in an earlier Western and dyed them brown for The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly (1966) and Once Upon a Time in the West (1968).[1] John Woo's A Better Tomorrow (1986) popularised long coats in Hong Kong films, and characters such as Omar Little in The Wire later wore dusters.[1] Leather dusters are also worn by motorcyclists.[1]

timeline.event: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly brings the duster back to screen.[1]
A Better Tomorrow popularises long coats in Hong Kong cinema.[1]
